readerTitle: Why a plumber's best salesperson might be a home inspector
caseNote: 가상 사례 (배관 업체와 주택 점검사, 보험사 안의 신규 상품팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 파트너십은 남이 이미 만들어 둔 자산(고객 접점, 신뢰, 역량)을 빌리는 일이다. 직접 만드는 비용과 시간이 빌리는 비용보다 클 때 파트너를 찾는다.
misconception: 수익을 나눠 주면 손해다. 혼자 다 하면 판매 한 건에서 더 많이 남는다.

sources.text: 경영 전략의 표준 개념 (make-or-buy, build vs. partner 판단)

factChecks.note: 월 10건 기준: 광고비 $120 × 10 = $1,200, 소개 수수료 $60 × 10 = $600. 점검사가 월 40가구를 만나고 그중 25%가 예약한다는 가정(40 × 0.25 = 10건).
모든 수치와 업체, 팀은 가상입니다. 특정 업종의 평균 고객 획득 비용을 나타내지 않습니다.

cards.title: Why a plumber's best salesperson might be a home inspector
body: A small plumbing company pays about $120 in online ads to win each new customer.
A local home inspector meets 40 new homeowners a month. Many of them will need a plumber soon. She offers to send them your way for $60 per booked job.
Giving away part of every job feels like losing money. Let's check.

image.label: A home inspector handing a plumber's card to new homeowners
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 새 집 현관 앞에서 점검사가 클립보드를 들고 젊은 부부에게 배관공 명함을 건네는 장면. 뒤편에 작은 배관 트럭. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where should your next new customers come from?
body: Your average first job is $300. Parts and labor cost $150. You want 10 more new customers a month.
Which path do you choose?

options.text: Spend more on your own ads, so you keep the whole job
options.feedback: You keep full control, but each customer costs $120, twice the inspector's fee. Keeping the whole job is not the same as keeping more money.

options.text: Take the inspector's offer and pay $60 per booked job
options.feedback: You pay for customers only when they book, and at half the cost. You do give up some control over how many referrals arrive.

options.text: Hire a salesperson to knock on doors in new neighborhoods
options.feedback: You build reach you own, which lasts. But a salary starts on day one, and it may take months to match what the inspector already has.

cards.title: Sharing the job leaves you three times more.
body: Ads: $300 − $150 − $120 = **$30** left from each first job.
For 10 customers a month, that's $600 in fees instead of $1,200 in ads.

cards.title: Partner to borrow what's already built.
body: A **partnership** lets you use something another business has already built, such as customers, trust or a skill, instead of building it yourself.
The question is simple: what would it cost, in money and time, to build this myself? If borrowing is cheaper and faster, partner.
The inspector spent years earning homeowners' trust. You get to use it for $60.

image.label: Two paths: building a bridge yourself vs. using an existing one
image.brief: 두 갈래 길 인포그래픽. 왼쪽은 "Build it yourself" 라벨과 함께 공사 중인 다리(시간·비용 아이콘), 오른쪽은 "Borrow it" 라벨과 함께 이미 완성된 다리를 건너는 배관공. 로고 없음.

cards.title: It's cheap for them, costly for you.
body: Most partnerships borrow one of three things:
list: **Trust:** a reputation that makes customers say yes
**Capability:** a skill or tool you'd need years to build
cards.callout: For the inspector, passing on a name costs almost nothing. For you, earning that trust from scratch costs a lot. That gap is where partnerships pay.
cards.softwareNote: A small software tool can spend heavily to find users, or integrate with a larger platform its target users already open every day. The platform's audience is the borrowed asset.

cards.title: A good partnership is not a favor.
body: The inspector isn't helping you out of kindness. Recommending a reliable plumber makes her own service more useful, and the fee is extra income for work she's already doing.
If only one side gains, the deal fades. Before you ask, work out what the partner gets and why it's cheap for them to give.

cards.title: What you borrow can be taken back.
body: The inspector can switch to another plumber tomorrow. If most of your customers come through her, she sets the terms.
So ask whether the asset is core to your business. Borrow what's nice to have. Build what you can't afford to lose.
Partnerships also take time: calls, updates, fixing mistakes. Count that cost too.

cards.title: Now you lead a new team inside an insurer.
body: Your team launched a policy for small business owners. The company's regional sales team already visits about 2,000 small business clients a year, but your product isn't their priority.
How do you reach those customers?

options.text: Hire two salespeople of your own; it takes about six months
options.feedback: You'd own the reach and control the pitch. But you'd pay to rebuild access the company already has, and lose half a year.

options.text: Offer the regional team credit toward their targets for each policy they sell
options.feedback: You borrow relationships they've already built, and they gain something they care about. You give up some control over how your product is pitched.

options.text: Email the regional team's clients directly without involving them
options.feedback: It's fast and cheap. But you'd spend their trust without asking, and likely lose the team as a partner.

cards.softwareNote: The same logic applies to software teams inside big companies: reusing another team's sign-up flow or data is often faster than building your own, if they gain something too.

cards.title: Before you build it, ask who already has it.
body: A partner's share looks like lost money. Compared with the cost and time of building the same thing, it's often the cheaper path.
**Try it today:** name one thing you need to grow, like customers, trust or a skill. Write down who already has it and what it would cost them to share.
